lesson.title: A Shortcut Written in Noble Gas
lesson.summary: Noble gas notation abbreviates a full electron configuration by replacing the core electrons with the symbol of the preceding noble gas in brackets, leaving only the valence electrons written out explicitly.
lesson.body:
Full electron configurations get long fast. Iron, atomic number 26, has the complete configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6, which is accurate but tedious to write every time, especially for elements much larger than iron. Since you now know that core electrons for any main group or transition element almost always duplicate the complete configuration of the nearest preceding noble gas exactly, there is an obvious shortcut available: replace that entire repeated block with the noble gas's chemical symbol in square brackets, and write out only the remaining valence electrons in full.

Applying this to chlorine, whose full configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5, the ten core electrons (1s2 2s2 2p6) exactly match neon's full configuration, so noble gas notation writes chlorine as [Ne] 3s2 3p5. Both notations describe the identical atom with the identical 17 electrons; the shorthand version simply hides the part that is guaranteed to be the same as neon's own configuration, letting you see the chemically important valence electrons, 3s2 3p5, at a glance.

Iron, mentioned above, shows how much the shortcut saves for a heavier element. The nearest noble gas below iron on the periodic table is argon, atomic number 18, with configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6. Iron's 26 electrons include those same 18 as an exact match, leaving 26 minus 18, or 8 more electrons to place, which fill as 4s2 3d6 (2 plus 6 equals 8, the correct remaining count). So iron in noble gas notation is [Ar] 4s2 3d6, a much shorter and, once you know the trick, equally informative way of writing the same 26 electron atom, since anyone reading it can immediately tell that only the 4s and 3d electrons are chemically relevant.

Building a noble gas notation configuration always follows the same three step process. First, find the largest noble gas whose atomic number is still smaller than the element you are working with, and put its symbol in brackets. Second, subtract that noble gas's atomic number from your element's atomic number to find out how many electrons still need placing. Third, continue filling subshells from exactly where that noble gas configuration left off, following the same Aufbau order, Pauli capacity limits, and Hund's rule distribution you already use for full configurations, until every remaining electron has a home.

Noble gas notation is not just a space saving trick; it visually foregrounds exactly the electrons that matter most for chemical behavior, the valence electrons, while compressing the chemically inert core into a single bracketed symbol. That makes it the preferred way chemists write configurations for anything past the second row of the periodic table, and it is also the natural starting point for working out what happens to an atom's configuration when it gains or loses electrons to form an ion, which is exactly the next topic.
